concept.shortExplanation: A loss function is the only place where you get to say what 'wrong' means. Everything else in training is mechanical: the optimiser will minimise whatever number you hand it, faithfully and without judgement. Squared error punishes big misses disproportionately, absolute error does not, and cross-entropy punishes confident wrong answers far more harshly than hesitant ones. Choosing badly here produces a model that succeeds at the wrong task.
concept.ahaMoment: Outlier sensitivity was never a property of your model — it was a property of the loss you picked. Swapping squared error for absolute error changes the answer without changing a single thing about the architecture.

levels.title: Minimise by Hand
levels.instructions: Move the prediction line to minimise mean squared error against the data points. The loss readout is computed live from your current position.
hints: Look at how much y grows each time x increases by 1 — that growth rate is your slope. Then check where the line should sit when x=0 for your intercept.
From x=0 to x=4, y climbs from about 1.1 to about 9.1 — roughly 2 units of y per 1 unit of x. That puts the intercept, the value at x=0, close to 1.
Slope ≈ 2.0, intercept ≈ 1.0 (precisely, about 1.99 and 1.04) — that's the true least-squares fit and lands in three-star range.

levels.title: The Outlier
levels.instructions: One point is a clear outlier. Fit the same line under squared error and under absolute error, and see which one the outlier drags. Match the target fit under absolute error.
hints: Four of the five points sit exactly on a clean line — find that line first, then decide how much the fifth (outlier) point should be allowed to pull it.

Under absolute error, one huge miss costs proportionally the same per unit as several small misses — it doesn't get squared into dominance. That means the line barely needs to move to accommodate the outlier at all.

Slope = 1, intercept = 1 (the exact line through the four normal points) gives MAE = 2.0, comfortably inside three stars — the outlier's own error is large (10) but MAE only counts it linearly, not quadratically.

levels.title: Pick the Right Loss
levels.instructions: Each scenario describes a real task. Choose the loss function that encodes what actually matters in that setting.

scenarios.prompt: Predicting house prices where a handful of mansions skew the dataset badly.
Classifying whether an email is spam, and you need calibrated probabilities out.
A margin-based classifier where you only care about examples near the boundary.
Forecasting temperature, where every error matters in proportion to its square.

hints: Ask what each scenario actually punishes: does it care about outliers proportionally, quadratically, about calibrated confidence, or only about examples near a decision boundary?

Mansions skewing house prices badly is a call for a loss that doesn't overreact to big misses. Needing calibrated probabilities points to the loss built for probabilities. 'Only care about examples near the boundary' names a loss by its own definition.
House prices with outliers → MAE. Calibrated spam probabilities → cross-entropy. Margin-based, boundary-only → hinge. Every-error-matters-squared temperature forecasting → MSE.
